comments.author: @DavidMartin-x5k
comments.text: The modern economic system has been redesigned to abuse regular people for corporate profit, destroying the foundational stability we had in the 1970s and 1980s. We used to have a society where a single working parent could own a decent home, support a family, and rely on a secure 30-year pension backed by local factories that anchored the community. Today, that human-centric world has been replaced by a predatory machine that demands infinite stock market growth at the expense of human dignity. To feed this corporate greed, prices must rise every single year, meaning workers spend 30 to 40 years paying hyper-inflated costs that quietly erase the value of their long-term savings. The painful results are all around us: constant layoffs, stagnant wages, shrinking packages, and deteriorating quality. Wall Street is even invading our towns by buying up independent roofing companies and veterinary clinics, driving costs up and wiping out the local businesses that used to treat people like neighbors instead of disposable assets. No one can honestly argue things are better now; we have traded a lifetime of real, daily peace for an exhausting system that forces people to live broke just to support institutional greed.

comments.author: @DavidMartin-x5k
comments.text:
By ruthlessly squeezing working families for maximum profit, the corporate world is accidentally creating the exact outcome it fears most: a massive public push toward socialism and government intervention.When mega-corporations price everyday people out of basic survival needs like healthcare and housing, voters lose faith in the free market. Left with no way to survive, millions of people naturally demand that the government step in to cap prices, punish corporate greed, and fund public alternatives. We cannot indefinitely siphon wealth from the foundation of its own consumer base without eventually collapsing under its own weight. Economists call this structural breaking point "demand destruction," and we are seeing the early stages of it right now as everyday people are forced to opt out of the commercial economy just to survive. The disconnect between a struggling public and a rising stock market happens because the stock market is not the economy—it only reflects the profits of the largest corporations, which are actively benefiting from the high prices squeezing everyday families...

In the 80's family-owned businesses were the backbone of American towns. The passage of NAFTA in 1994 marked a massive turning point, shifting the country away from community-centered economies and laying the groundwork for the highly globalized, corporate-dominated financial system we have today. That capitalism then was great not this mess we have today. 

When a handful of mega-companies control the majority of our food, housing, and insurance, they possess the leverage to extract every spare dollar from the public, completely detached from traditional supply and demand.
